title: Rabbi Joshua Keeps the People's Day
hook: a sage keeps Yom Kippur on the court's day, not his own
carry: the holy days belong to the whole people

segments.voice: Noa's college calendar arrived: move-in, midterms, finals. She laid it next to the Jewish calendar and groaned. Yom Kippur lands on her first chemistry quiz. Couldn't she just keep it a day later, on her own? Who decides which day is holy? The Mishnah tells of a great sage who had to answer that the hard way.
screen: `MOVE-IN. MIDTERMS. FINALS.` → `YOM KIPPUR ON QUIZ DAY.` → `WHO DECIDES WHICH DAY IS HOLY?`

segments.voice: The Torah calls the festivals mo'adim, appointed seasons, "which ye shall proclaim in their appointed season." Proclaim. In those days the court declared each new month when witnesses saw the new moon, and the festivals followed. One year, Rabbi Joshua was sure the court's head, Rabban Gamliel, had accepted the wrong witnesses. By his own count, Yom Kippur fell on a different day. So Rabban Gamliel ordered him: come to me with your staff and your money on the day you count as Yom Kippur. Things you'd never carry on the holiest day. Rabbi Joshua was crushed. Rabbi Akiva found him troubled and comforted him with the verse: which you shall proclaim. The days are the ones the court proclaims. So Rabbi Joshua took his staff and his money and walked. And Rabban Gamliel stood, kissed him on the head, and said: come in peace, my teacher and my student. Here's the teaching. Jewish holy days aren't a private schedule. They're appointed for the whole people together. Today the Hebrew calendar is worked out in advance, so Jews everywhere fast on the same Yom Kippur. Your year is your share of that one calendar, kept even when a quiz lands on it. Something to tell a friend tonight: a sage carried his wallet on his own Yom Kippur so the people would keep one day together.

segments.voice: Open a calendar and find this year's Yom Kippur, or the next festival. Mark it the way you'd mark something you can't move. Then name the people keeping that same day with you, near or far, and the one thing you'll do now so you can keep it with them.

segments.voice: Your year: the festivals you keep, appointed seasons proclaimed for the whole people, kept in your real life.
Here's the line: the holy days belong to the whole people, and your year is your share. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Jewish year runs on the Hebrew calendar, once set month by month by a court and now calculated in advance, so Jews everywhere keep the same festival days; students and workers ask for time off ahead, or find a seder, a sukkah or a break-fast near where they are.

Yom Kippur.meaning: the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and prayer

Pesach.meaning: Passover, the festival of the Exodus from Egypt

mo'adim.meaning: appointed seasons: the Torah's name for the festivals

Rabbi Joshua.meaning: Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, a leading sage of the Mishnah

Rabban Gamliel.meaning: head of the rabbinic court at Yavneh

Rabbi Akiva.meaning: a great sage and teacher of the Mishnah's era

seder.meaning: the Passover meal, told in order
